simple: the rules that let two pieces of already-compiled code work together.
analogy: the exact layout of every form at the office window.
precise: the machine-level contract between separately compiled components: calling convention, data type sizes and alignment, structure layouts, object-file format and, for an operating system, how programs request kernel services and how processes start.

simple: the exact way a program asks the kernel for something.
analogy: the office's form catalogue: form numbers, boxes, reply slips.
precise: the instruction used to enter the kernel, the register that carries the call number, the registers that carry arguments and the result, the numbering of calls, the layout of structures passed through memory, and the error convention.

simple: the number that says which service you want.

analogy: pushing the form through the window.

simple: the C library's variable that holds the reason for the last failure.
analogy: the refusal reason written on the reply slip, copied into your notebook.
precise: an integer lvalue defined by the C standard and POSIX; functions that fail set it to a positive error number such as EBADF; it is per thread in POSIX.

simple: how a kernel says "no" and why.
analogy: the refusal slip's format.
precise: the rule for encoding failure in the result; Linux returns minus the error number in the result register, which the C library turns into −1 and errno (observed in R1).

simple: the answer "there is no such service".
analogy: "we do not have a form with that number".
precise: the error a Linux kernel returns, as −ENOSYS, for a system-call number it does not implement; the header comment asks real system calls not to return it, so callers can tell "missing" from "failed".

simple: a compiler, assembler and linker that know your OS by name.
analogy: the printer who has your school on its list.
precise: GCC with Binutils, or Clang with LLD, patched so the triple <arch>-<yourOS> selects your start files, libraries, search paths, predefined macros and defaults.
source: C1 of F3-54 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (rows "A toolchain that targets your OS" and "Build systems and ports") and milestone U4 (goal, read and build lists, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4); D2 of F3-54 (LLVM documentation on target triples and Clang's driver and toolchain classes (curriculum section 8.1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a folder that looks like the root of your OS, holding its headers and libraries.
analogy: the school's own pictures and timetables, sent to the printer.
precise: a directory tree the compiler and linker treat as the target's root for header and library search (usr/include, usr/lib), so nothing from the build host is used.
source: C1 of F3-54 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (rows "A toolchain that targets your OS" and "Build systems and ports") and milestone U4 (goal, read and build lists, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4); R3 of F3-54 (the sysroot, the wrapper and the first program (sysroot.log, hello_myos.log); clang 18.1.3, LLD 18, GNU Binutils 2.42) — lab run in this build

simple: the gcc or clang command itself, which runs the compiler, assembler and linker for you.
analogy: the print-shop clerk who sends the order to each machine.
precise: the program that turns one command line into a sequence of tool invocations, choosing start files, libraries and linker options per target; in Clang, chosen through per-OS "toolchain" classes.
source: D2 of F3-54 (LLVM documentation on target triples and Clang's driver and toolchain classes (curriculum section 8.1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F3-54 (Clang's triples, macros and planned link step (triple_clang.log, driver_trap.log); clang 18.1.3) — lab run in this build

simple: a collection of recipes, one per program, that say how to build it for your OS.
analogy: the print room's order list with "print after" notes.
precise: per package: source location and checksum, patches, dependencies, configure/build/install steps into a staging folder, and packaging; examples named by the curriculum are SerenityOS's Ports, managarm's bootstrap recipes driven by xbstrap, and NetBSD's pkgsrc.
source: C1 of F3-54 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (rows "A toolchain that targets your OS" and "Build systems and ports") and milestone U4 (goal, read and build lists, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4)

simple: an order in which every recipe comes after the recipes it needs.
analogy: print the reader before the workbook.
precise: a topological sort of the dependency graph; grouping into "waves" of recipes whose dependencies are all in earlier waves shows what may build in parallel; a cycle makes an order impossible.
source: R4 of F3-54 (Listing 3 with both trees (ports.log: exit code 0; ports_broken.log: exit code 1, expected)) — lab run in this build

simple: building the same sources twice gives exactly the same bytes.
analogy: two print runs of the same workbook are indistinguishable.
precise: byte-identical outputs from the same sources, toolchain and recipe, independent of time, user, folder and machine; U4 asks for byte-identical packages on a second machine "or the differences are explained".
source: C1 of F3-54 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (rows "A toolchain that targets your OS" and "Build systems and ports") and milestone U4 (goal, read and build lists, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4); R5 of F3-54 (the reproducibility comparison (repro.log); GNU tar) — lab run in this build

simple: an agreed "build time" that tools use instead of the clock.
analogy: the edition date printed in the book instead of the day it went through the press.
precise: an environment variable holding a Unix time; in this build Clang used it for __DATE__ and __TIME__ (R6).
source: R6 of F3-54 (the forensic evidence and the fixed build (forensic_repro.log, forensic_fixed.log)) — lab run in this build; D5 of F3-54 (Reproducible-builds documentation on sources of non-determinism and the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH specification) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system that can rebuild itself with tools running on itself.
analogy: a school that trains its own teachers.
precise: in the curriculum, U5: "The compiler runs inside your OS and the system can rebuild itself", graded in five levels from a native "hello" to a compiler that rebuilds itself.
source: C1 of F3-55 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (row "Self-hosting"), section 8.2 (levels of self-hosting) and milestone U5 (goal, build list, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4)

simple: where a compiler is built, where it runs, and what it makes programs for.
analogy: where the teacher was trained, where she teaches, and which pupils she teaches.
precise: the three system types of GNU configure: --build (the machine doing the build), --host (the machine the result runs on), --target (for compilers: the machine the result generates code for).
source: D1 of F3-55 (GCC installation documentation (configuration: build, host and target; native builds; bootstrap with stage comparison) and GCC sources (curriculum item 138)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F3-55 (build, host and target of three installed compilers (triples.log)) — lab run in this build

simple: a compiler that makes programs for the same system it runs on.
analogy: a teacher teaching at the school where she now works.
precise: host equals target; in U5, host and target are your OS.
source: D1 of F3-55 (GCC installation documentation (configuration: build, host and target; native builds; bootstrap with stage comparison) and GCC sources (curriculum item 138)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: building, on one machine, a compiler that will run on a second machine.
analogy: the outside college preparing a teacher who will work at your school.
precise: a build where build, host and target are not all equal and build differs from host; the usual way to produce the first native compiler for a new OS: build = Linux, host = target = your OS.
source: D1 of F3-55 (GCC installation documentation (configuration: build, host and target; native builds; bootstrap with stage comparison) and GCC sources (curriculum item 138)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: building a compiler with itself, twice, and checking the two results are the same.
analogy: the inspector's word-for-word lesson comparison.
precise: GCC's native bootstrap: stage 1 built by the existing compiler, stage 2 built by stage 1, stage 3 built by stage 2; the object files of stages 2 and 3 are compared ("stage comparison"); the curriculum lists it as U5's stretch goal.
source: D1 of F3-55 (GCC installation documentation (configuration: build, host and target; native builds; bootstrap with stage comparison) and GCC sources (curriculum item 138)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); C1 of F3-55 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 8.1 (row "Self-hosting"), section 8.2 (levels of self-hosting) and milestone U5 (goal, build list, acceptance tests quoted verbatim)) — a map, not a source (AH-4)

simple: comparing two builds of the compiler byte for byte.
analogy: comparing two teachers' lessons word for word.
precise: a check that two compiler binaries built from the same sources by functionally equivalent compilers are identical; a difference points to a miscompilation, non-determinism or an environment leak.
source: D1 of F3-55 (GCC installation documentation (configuration: build, host and target; native builds; bootstrap with stage comparison) and GCC sources (curriculum item 138)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-55 (the stage comparison in miniature (university/labs/F3-55/stage_compare.log, minicc.log); g++ 13.3.0, clang 18.1.3, GNU Binutils 2.42) — lab run in this build

simple: the g++ command starts several programs one after another.
analogy: the timetable that sends a class from room to room.
precise: in this build, g++ started cc1plus (the C++ compiler proper) and as (the assembler) for one -c compile, communicating through a temporary assembly file.
source: R2 of F3-55 (the trace of one compile (compile_trace.log); strace 6.8, g++ 13.3.0) — lab run in this build
